questions.question: What is the difference between DOMContentLoaded and load?
questions.title: DOMContentLoaded versus load
questions.direct_answer: DOMContentLoaded fires after the HTML has been parsed and deferred or module scripts have executed; it does not wait for images, subframes, or async scripts. The window load event fires later, after the document and most dependent resources have finished loading.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of document readiness and choosing the correct lifecycle event.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Waiting for load before initializing code that only needs the DOM, or registering too late for DOMContentLoaded.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Asynchronous or dynamically loaded code must inspect document.readyState because DOMContentLoaded may already have fired.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: DOMContentLoaded means the DOM has been parsed and deferred scripts have run.
It does not wait for images, subframes, or async scripts.
load is for work that needs the document's dependent resources to finish.
Late-running code should check document.readyState before waiting.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
- `DOMContentLoaded` and `load` mark different readiness levels. DOMContentLoaded fires when the HTML document has been completely parsed and deferred classic scripts and module scripts have executed.

- It does not wait for resources such as images or subframes, and it does not wait for async scripts. The window `load` event happens later, when the document and its dependent resources have completed loading.

- For example, code that wires a click listener to an existing button only needs the DOM, so a deferred script can initialize directly or use DOMContentLoaded. Code that measures an image's natural dimensions may need that image's own load state.

- A dynamically imported or async module may begin after DOMContentLoaded has already occurred. It should check `document.readyState`: register a listener while the state is `loading`, otherwise run initialization immediately.

- Use the earliest milestone that satisfies the dependency. Waiting for load by default delays usable behaviour without adding correctness.

sections.title: Readiness is a set of milestones
sections.content: The parser, scripts, styles, images, fonts, and frames do not finish at one instant. Lifecycle events expose useful boundaries in that work. A component should depend on the resource it actually needs instead of treating the entire page as one indivisible load.

sections.title: Why a readyState guard is reliable
sections.content: JavaScript tasks run to completion. If readyState is `loading` during the check, the document cannot finish parsing in the middle of that same task before the listener is attached. If parsing already finished, immediate initialization avoids waiting for an event that will not fire again. An idempotent setup function also prevents accidental double registration.

sections.title: Typical readiness order
sections.content:
HTML parsing
   ↓ deferred and module scripts finish
DOMContentLoaded
   ↓ images, subframes, and other dependent resources finish
window load

Async script execution can occur independently of DOMContentLoaded.

questions.question: How do async and defer change classic script loading?
questions.title: async versus defer scripts
questions.direct_answer: For external classic scripts, both async and defer allow downloading while HTML parsing continues. An async script executes as soon as it is ready without preserving document order, while deferred scripts execute after parsing in document order and before DOMContentLoaded.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of script download, execution order, and parser interaction.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using async for dependent scripts or assuming defer has the same effect on inline classic scripts.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Module scripts are deferred by default and have their own dependency graph; the classic-script rules should not be copied blindly to modules.

sections.title: Quick revision
items: Both attributes avoid blocking HTML parsing during download.
async executes when ready and does not preserve document order.
defer executes after parsing and preserves document order.
DOMContentLoaded waits for deferred classic scripts, not async scripts.

sections.title: Interview answer
sections.content:
- On external classic scripts, `async` and `defer` both let fetching happen while the HTML parser continues. The difference is when execution happens and whether document order is preserved.

- An async script executes as soon as its download is ready. It can interrupt parsing, independent async scripts may execute in any order, and DOMContentLoaded does not wait for them.

- A deferred script waits until HTML parsing has finished, then deferred scripts execute in document order before DOMContentLoaded. That makes defer a natural choice for an application bundle that depends on the parsed DOM or on an earlier deferred library.

- For example, an independent analytics script can often be async, while `vendor.js` followed by `app.js` can use defer when the application requires that order. A normal classic script with neither attribute blocks parsing while it is fetched and executed.

- These rules describe external classic scripts. Inline defer has no useful delaying effect, and module scripts are deferred by default unless their own async behaviour is requested.

sections.title: Download and execution are separate decisions
sections.content: A parser-blocking script couples both activities to the current parser position. async separates download but executes at the first opportunity. defer separates download and also postpones execution until the document has been parsed. Choosing correctly prevents both a blank parser stall and an accidental dependency race.

sections.title: Dependency order determines the attribute
sections.content: async works only when a script can run independently of neighbouring scripts and of a particular parsed element. defer creates a predictable sequence across deferred classic scripts in document order. Modern bundles may use modules, dynamic imports, preload hints, or framework-specific bootstrapping, but the same question remains: what must exist before this code can execute correctly?

sections.title: Classic external script timing
sections.content:
| Form | Downloads | Executes | Order |
|---|---|---|---|
| `<script src>` | Parser waits | Immediately when fetched | Document order |
| `<script async src>` | During parsing | As soon as ready | Not guaranteed |
| `<script defer src>` | During parsing | After parsing, before DOMContentLoaded | Document order |

sections.title: Choose attributes from dependencies
sections.content:
```html
<script async src="analytics.js"></script>
<script defer src="vendor.js"></script>
<script defer src="app.js"></script>
```
`analytics.js` is independent; the two deferred scripts retain their document order.
